summary: This note explains how rainbows form, describing the physical phenomena of reflection, refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection (TIR) as sunlight interacts with raindrops. It walks through seven steps from sunlight striking a raindrop to the final further dispersion of colours as light leaves the drop. The note is a copyrighted 1999 educational page by Rebecca McDowell with ray diagrams and an overview.
one_line: Explains the seven-step physics of rainbow formation in raindrops, covering reflection, refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection.
key_facts: Rainbow formation involves reflection, refraction, dispersion and total internal reflection.
These phenomena occur due to the interaction of light with air and water and the boundaries between them.
White light from the Sun must hit raindrops at a certain angle before a rainbow is possible.
The sun is best fairly low in the sky, such as at dawn and late afternoon, for rainbows.
When light passes from air into water it slows down because water is denser than air, causing refraction toward the normal line.
White light is made up of a spectrum of colours, each with its own wavelength.
Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths travel at different speeds and separate when entering a medium of different density.
At the rear of the raindrop, Total Internal Reflection occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
A rainbow is only seen if Total Internal Reflection happens; otherwise light exits the far side and moves away from the viewer.
As light leaves the raindrop from water into air, it speeds up and its path bends away from the normal line.
The overall result of the second refraction is increased separation of the component colours of white light.
The page is copyright 1999 by Rebecca McDowell.
